items.title: Ethnic Differences in Clinical Manifestations of Behçet's Disease: A Retrospective Cohort Study of Turkic and Non-Turkic Patients.
items.abstract: Behçet's disease (BD) is a multisystem inflammatory vasculitis with clinical heterogeneity that may vary across ethnic groups within the same country. This study aimed to evaluate the influence of ethnicity on the clinical manifestations, immunogenic laboratory findings and disease course of BD by comparing Turkic and non-Turkic patients in a large Iranian referral cohort. In this retrospective cohort study, 2697 patients with BD followed at the BD clinic of Shariati Hospital in Tehran, Iran, from 2007 to 2019 were included. Patients were stratified by ethnicity into Turkic (N = 1037; 38.5%) and non-Turkic (N = 1660; 61.5% [with Persian/Fars, N = 980 subgrouping]) groups, and demographic, clinical manifestations, and immunogenic laboratory findings were extracted from medical records. Mean age at BD onset was 25.72 ± 10.02 years in Turkic patients and 24.69 ± 10.23 years in non-Turkic patients, and males comprised 61.3% and 57.1% of the two groups, respectively. Human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-B5 positivity was 55.1% in Turkic versus 53.1% in non-Turkic patients, and HLA-B51 positivity was 48.7% versus 46.5%, respectively. Most clinical manifestations showed similar prevalence across groups, including oral aphthous ulcers (98.7% vs. 99.0%), genital aphthous ulcers (60.5% vs. 62.0%), uveitis (50.1% vs. 53.2%), and deep vein thrombosis (5.3% vs. 5.1%). Superficial phlebitis was more frequent in Turkic patients (p = 0.02), and oral aphthous ulcers occurred earlier in Turkic patients (p = 0.023). A three-class latent class model demonstrated the best fit (BIC = 14,986.58). In multinomial logistic regression analysis, Turkic patients had slightly higher odds ratio of the ocular-predominant phenotype (OR = 1.10, 95% CI: 0.91-1.33; p = 0.320) and slightly lower odds ratio of the multisystem phenotype (OR = 0.94, 95% CI: 0.68-1.30; p = 0.692); however, neither association was statistically significant. Female gender was associated with higher odds ratio of the ocular-predominant phenotype than the mucocutaneous-predominant phenotype (OR = 1.38, 95% CI: 1.14-1.67; p = 0.001). In this large Iranian BD cohort, Turkic and non-Turkic patients exhibited broadly similar disease phenotypes and comparable HLA-B51 frequencies, with small but potentially relevant ethnic differences in the timing of oral ulcers and the frequency of superficial phlebitis. These findings suggest that ethnicity may influence BD phenotype through mechanisms beyond HLA-B51, possibly involving other immune-related genetic variants such as tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α, endoplasmic reticulum aminopeptidase 1(ERAP1), Interleukin (IL)-10. Of note, the significant differences observed in Turkic versus non-Turkic comparisons were not present in the Turkic versus Persian (Fars) comparison, indicating that the findings are not driven by a single ethnic subgroup.

items.title: Identification and Validation of Hub Genes Associated With Periodontitis and Systemic Lupus Erythematosus.
items.abstract: Accumulating evidence suggests a close relationship between periodontitis and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE); however, the shared molecular mechanisms underlying this association remain unclear. This study aimed to identify candidate genes and molecular features shared between periodontitis and SLE through integrative bioinformatics analysis and clinical validation. Gene expression profiles were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database, and differentially expressed genes (DEGs) shared between periodontitis and SLE were identified. Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses were performed, followed by protein-protein interaction (PPI) network construction and hub gene screening. The expression patterns of the hub genes were evaluated in independent validation datasets, and their discriminatory performance was assessed by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Immune cell infiltration and its correlations with hub gene expression were further investigated. Transcription factor-microRNA regulatory networks and candidate compounds were computationally predicted. Finally, quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR) was performed to validate hub gene expression in clinical samples. A total of 124 overlapping DEGs were identified, from which five hub genes-CCL3, LY96, FOS, MMP9, and PTGS2-were selected. GO and KEGG enrichment analyses indicated that the overlapping DEGs were predominantly associated with inflammatory and immune-related biological processes and signaling pathways. All five hub genes showed consistent expression patterns in the independent periodontitis validation dataset, whereas FOS, LY96, and PTGS2, but not CCL3 and MMP9, showed consistent differential expression in the independent SLE validation dataset. ROC analyses demonstrated varying discriminatory performance across the analyzed datasets. Immune infiltration analysis revealed differences in estimated immune cell profiles in both disease datasets, and computational prediction identified candidate regulatory interactions and compounds for further investigation. qPCR validation in clinical samples (n = 15 per group) showed significantly increased expression of all five hub genes in gingival tissues from patients with periodontitis and PBMCs from patients with SLE compared with their respective healthy controls. This study identified CCL3, LY96, FOS, MMP9, and PTGS2 as candidate genes associated with periodontitis and SLE. FOS, LY96, and PTGS2 showed consistent expression patterns across datasets, whereas CCL3 and MMP9 exhibited dataset-dependent variation in SLE. Clinical qPCR validation showed increased expression of all five genes in both disease cohorts. These findings provide insight into the shared molecular features of periodontitis and SLE and warrant further validation in larger, independent, and clinically well-characterized cohorts.

items.title: Evaluation of factors affecting physical activity and physical function in women with primary sjogren syndrome.
items.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the factors affecting physical activity and physical function in primary Sjogren syndrome. In total, 63 women with primary Sjogren syndrome were examined for physical activity using the International Physical Activity Questionnaire, identified barriers to activity via the Self-Perceived Barriers for Physical Activity Questionnaire, and assessed physical function with the 30-s sit-to-stand and grip strength tests. Disease activity was measured with the EULAR Sjögren's Syndrome Disease Activity Index, symptom severity with the EULAR Sjogren's Syndrome Patient Reported Index, and fatigue using the Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory. Anxiety and depression levels were evaluated with the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, while health perception was assessed with the Health Perception Scale. A one-unit increase in the HPS_Center of control score was associated with a 23.1-point increase in the median International Physical Activity Questionnaire total score (95%CIs 0.55; 63.52). An increase in the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale-Anxiety, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale-Depression, and MFI_total scores is associated with a rise in the Self-Perceived Barriers for Physical Activity Questionnaire score (0.69 [0.42; 1.13]), (1.07 [0.58; 1.41]), and (0.25 [0.1; 0.3]), respectively. Conversely, grip strength was associated with EULAR Sjogren's Syndrome Patient Reported Index, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale-Depression, and MFI_Reduced Motivation (-0.44 [-0.86; -0.01]), (-0.26 [-0.41; -0.08]), and (-0.22 [-0.48; -0.08]), respectively. However, the HPS_Self-awareness score had a positive effect on the 30-s sit-to-stand (0.18 [0.11; 0.3]). In women with primary Sjogren syndrome, emotional symptoms and fatigue were negatively associated with physical activity and function. Better health perception was positively associated with both. Health education and management of emotional disorders and fatigue can improve physical activity and function in primary Sjogren syndrome.

items.title: Psychological Experiences of Adults with Rheumatoid Arthritis: A Systematic Review and Qualitative Evidence Synthesis.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) causes unpredictable pain, progressive joint damage, and visible deformities. These features give rise to emotional and relational challenges, including fear of disability, loss of independence, and struggles with identity and social roles. This meta-synthesis aimed to systematically synthesize qualitative evidence on the psychological experiences of patients with RA to inform holistic nursing care. This is a qualitative meta-synthesis. Two reviewers systematically searched six electronic databases (PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO, Web of Science, and Scopus) from inception to March 28, 2026, supplemented by reference list screening. English-language qualitative studies on the psychological experiences of adults with RA were included. Methodological quality was assessed using the Critical Appraisal Skills Program checklist. Reflexive thematic analysis was used for qualitative evidence synthesis. Reporting adhered to the PRISMA and ENTREQ guidelines. The protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261355146). Thirty-three studies including 663 participants from ten countries were included. Three themes and twelve subthemes were generated: negative emotional experiences (helplessness, fear, guilt, loneliness); self-identity and meaning-making (bodily alienation, role loss, causal attributions, acceptance); and psychological conflicts in interpersonal interactions (dependence vs autonomy, reversed family roles, perceived stigma and pressure to conceal, estrangement in clinical encounters). The psychological burden extends beyond depression and anxiety, involving embodied distress and relational difficulties, yet patients also actively reconstruct meaning. Healthcare professionals can attend to the specific fears, identity struggles, and interpersonal tensions that patients describe. Asking open-ended questions about the most difficult aspects of living with the condition, validating subjective experiences, involving family members in discussions about role adjustments, and reinforcing patients' own adaptive efforts may contribute to more holistic nursing assessment and individualized care.

items.title: Iron Metabolism-associated Biomarkers in Rheumatoid Arthritis: A Meta-analysis of Diagnostic Value and Anemia-related Changes.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is associated with profound alterations in iron metabolism, contributing to chronic inflammation, immune dysfunction, and, in some cases, the development of anemia. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated serum biomarkers of iron metabolism in RA patients compared to healthy controls and assessed differences between anemic and non-anemic RA subgroups. PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science were systematically searched up to December 2024. Nineteen studies (n = 1,640) were included for the RA versus healthy control analysis, and six studies (n = 325) for the anemia subgroup comparison. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed to calculate standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS), and meta-regression was used to explore sources of heterogeneity. RA patients had significantly elevated ferritin (SMD = 1.14, p < 0.01), IL-6 (SMD = 3.94, p < 0.01), hepcidin, sTFR, and TNF-α levels, and reduced serum iron (SMD = -1.30, p < 0.01) and transferrin saturation. Hepcidin and transferrin levels were not significantly different. In anemic RA patients, lower iron and higher hepcidin and TIBC levels were observed. Meta-regression analyses did not identify significant moderators of heterogeneity. This meta-analysis indicates that RA is linked to inflammation-induced iron dysregulation, characterized by elevated ferritin levels, diminished serum iron, and functional iron deficiency. These modifications occur independently of anemia; however, anemic individuals exhibit additional alterations, such as elevated hepcidin and TIBC levels. Iron metabolism biomarkers may possess diagnostic and therapeutic significance in rheumatoid arthritis, especially for inflammation-mediated pathways. RA is characterized by systemic iron dysregulation, including ferritin upregulation and functional iron deficiency, independent of anemia. These findings highlight potential targets for future therapeutic strategies and improved disease monitoring.

items.title: Early warning and risk assessment of cardiac involvement in dermatomyositis/polymyositis: from biomarkers to multimodal imaging.
items.abstract: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM) comprise a broad spectrum of clinical and pathological subtypes, including dermatomyositis (DM), anti-synthetase syndrome, immune-mediated necrotising myopathy (IMNM), overlap myositis, inclusion-body myositis, and polymyositis (PM). Among these, DM remains well-defined, whereas PM has become increasingly rare under current classification criteria. A significant number of early studies categorised patients collectively under the term "DM/PM". Cardiac involvement is recognised as a significant cause of mortality in these patients. The reported incidence of cardiac involvement in DM/PM varies widely and is frequently subclinical. The symptoms are frequently masked by manifestations in the skeletal muscles and the skin, which makes an early diagnosis difficult using conventional examination methods. Although endomyocardial biopsy is regarded as the gold standard, its invasive nature limits its clinical application. It is therefore imperative to establish an efficient framework for early warning and precise risk assessment of cardiac involvement in DM/PM. In this review, we summarize current and emerging evidence on serum biomarkers and multimodal imaging for the early identification and risk assessment of cardiac involvement in DM/PM. These advances are built on the evolving classification system for IIM.The integration of these tools with clinical high-risk factors is intended to facilitate the construction of a comprehensive risk assessment model. This integrated approach is intended to facilitate the early detection and treatment of cardiac involvement in DM/PM patients, thereby improving their prognosis.

items.title: Development of an IL-6- and Th1/Treg-based nomogram for identifying low bone mass in patients with rheumatoid arthritis.
items.abstract: This study aimed to analyze clinical and immunological characteristics in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) according to bone loss status, integrate traditional risk factors with immune-inflammatory indicators, and construct and validate an individualized nomogram for estimating the probability of concurrent BMD-defined low bone mass in patients with RA. A total of 442 patients with RA were enrolled and divided into normal bone mass (RA-N, n=219) and low bone mass (RA-LBM, n=223) groups based on bone mineral density values. Data on the clinical characteristics, laboratory parameters, peripheral blood lymphocyte subsets, and cytokine levels were collected for both groups. The Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) method was applied for multiple testing correction. Univariate logistic regression was used to screen relevant variables, and the random forest algorithm (mean decrease Gini importance ranking and out-of-bag error analysis) was employed to determine the optimal combination of variables. Multivariate logistic regression was performed to identify factors independently associated with low bone mass, based on which a nomogram for identifying concurrent low bone mass was constructed. The discriminative ability of the model was evaluated using the receiver operating characteristic curve, calibration was assessed using the calibration curve and Hosmer-Lemeshow test, and clinical net benefit was evaluated using decision curve analysis. Patients in the RA-LBM group exhibited significantly higher values for age, disease duration, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, aspartate aminotransferase/alanine aminotransferase ratio, and alkaline phosphatase, while body mass index (BMI), red blood cell count, hemoglobin levels, albumin levels, and albumin/globulin ratio were significantly lower than those in the RA-N group (BH-adjusted P<0.05). Immunological analysis revealed that interleukin-6 (IL-6) levels were significantly elevated in the RA-LBM group (BH-adjusted P<0.001), and the T helper 1 cell/regulatory T cell (Th1/Treg) ratio was also significantly increased (BH-adjusted P = 0.016). Random forest analysis followed by multivariate logistic regression ultimately identified age, Th1/Treg ratio, BMI, IL-6, albumin, and uric acid levels as factors independently associated with low bone mass in patients with RA (BH-adjusted P<0.05). Model 1 constructed based on these six variables achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.906 (95% CI: 0.877-0.935), which was significantly higher than that of model 2 containing only traditional risk factors (AUC = 0.861, P = 0.001). The AUCs of model 1 in the training and validation sets were 0.906 and 0.905, respectively. The Hosmer-Lemeshow test indicated good model calibration. Decision curve analysis showed that the model provided a higher net benefit than the treat-all and treat-none strategies across a range of threshold probabilities. This study integrates immune-inflammatory indicators, such as IL-6 and Th1/Treg ratio, with traditional risk factors to construct a nomogram for identifying concurrent BMD-defined low bone mass in patients with RA. The model showed favorable discrimination and calibration and may provide a useful tool for estimating the probability of concurrent low bone mass in this population.

items.title: Case Report: Sacrococcygeal teratoma with malignant transformation into mixed adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma following TNF-α inhibitor therapy for ankylosing spondylitis.
items.abstract: Adult sacrococcygeal teratoma (SCT) with malignant transformation is exceptionally rare, and its occurrence during long-term tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) inhibitor therapy has never been reported. This case firstly links prolonged TNF-α blockade-used for ankylosing spondylitis-with aggressive biphenotypic (i.e. adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)) transformation of congenital SCT. Serial biopsies over time enabled dynamic tracking of histological changes from adenocarcinoma toward SCC, a phenomenon not previously documented in malignant SCT. The concurrent TP53 and KRAS G12D mutations further distinguish this case and suggest a potential targeted therapeutic avenue. A 31-year-old woman with two prior resections of gluteal masses and six-year TNF-α inhibitor exposure presented with a recurrent gluteal mass. Imaging revealed a pelvic-sacral mass and a gluteal subcutaneous soft tissue mass. Biopsy of the pelvic tumour only described intestinal-type adenocarcinoma; however, subsequent gluteal biopsy disclosed mixed components of 65% SCC and 35% adenocarcinoma. The origin diagnosis was malignant SCT with adeno-squamous transformation, IV stage with pelvic and gluteal metastases. Unfortunately, the patient successively developed local recurrence at the sacrococcygeal region and widespread metastases involving liver, inguinal lymph nodes, bone, lungs, and kidneys, although multidisciplinary Interventions were administered including resection, chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Clinicians should learn two key lessons from this case. First, it is imperative to sustain vigilance for malignant transformation in patients with a history of recurrent SCT, and regular follow-up is strongly advised. Second, although current meta-analyses demonstrate no statistically significant association between TNF-α inhibitor exposure and overall malignancy risk, the physiological role of TNF-α in immune surveillance, together with relevant clinical guidelines, supports discontinuation of these agents upon diagnosis of a solid malignancy. In this case, given the aggressive tumor behavior and the availability of alternative agents for ankylosing spondylitis, we elected to pause TNF-α blockade as a precautionary, guideline-informed clinical judgment.

items.title: Associations between thyrotropin receptor antibody, rheumatoid autoantibodies, and disease activity in patients with rheumatoid arthritis: a retrospective cross-sectional study.
items.abstract: Thyrotropin receptor antibody (TRAb) frequently coexists with rheumatoid factor (RF) and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody (anti-CCP) in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), but its association with disease activity remains unclear. This study assessed the associations of TRAb and rheumatoid autoantibodies with DAS28-ESR in RA patients. This retrospective cross-sectional study enrolled 192 RA patients hospitalized at the First Affiliated Hospital of Guizhou University of Traditional Chinese Medicine between October 2024 and October 2025, all meeting the 2010 ACR/EULAR criteria. Patients were classified as TRAb-positive or TRAb-negative using the clinical cutoff of 1.75 IU/L. Associations between TRAb and DAS28-ESR were evaluated by Spearman correlation, restricted cubic spline (RCS) analysis, and multivariable linear regression. The primary analysis was repeated in euthyroid patients ( n  = 167). Interactions of TRAb with Ln(RF) and Ln(anti-CCP) were tested in all 192 patients, and an exploratory four-group comparison was performed in 138 patients with concordant antibody titers. TRAb correlated positively with DAS28-ESR ( ρ =0.36, P  < 0.001), and RCS analysis revealed a nonlinear association ( P  = 0.002 for nonlinear). hs-CRP, ESR, and DAS28-ESR were higher in TRAb-positive ( n  = 51) than TRAb-negative patients ( n  = 141; all P  < 0.001). After covariate adjustment, TRAb positivity remained independently associated with higher DAS28-ESR ( B  = 1.457, P  < 0.001), and the association persisted in euthyroid patients (4.9 vs. 4.1, P  < 0.001). TRAb showed a statistically significant interaction with Ln(anti-CCP) ( P  = 0.0014) and a borderline interaction with Ln(RF) ( P  = 0.046); DAS28-ESR was highest in TRAb-positive patients with high-titer autoantibodies. TRAb positivity was associated with higher disease activity and systemic inflammation in RA patients, including those with normal thyroid function, and the association strengthened with increasing rheumatoid autoantibody titers. The value of combined TRAb, RF, and anti-CCP testing for immune stratification in RA warrants prospective validation.

items.title: Metachronous sequential involvement of rice-body bursitis in the shoulder and knee: a case report of rare polyarticular presentation in a patient with rheumatoid arthritis.
items.abstract: Rice-body bursitis is an uncommon complication of rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Metachronous involvement of multiple joints has rarely been described. We report a 52-year-old woman with a 16-year history of RA who presented in 2019 with refractory swelling of the right shoulder. Ultrasound and MRI revealed "honeycomb-like" effusion and T2-hypointense particles within the subacromial-subdeltoid bursa, leading to a probable imaging-based diagnosis of rice-body bursitis. She achieved complete remission approximately 6 months after adalimumab was started, during which leflunomide was continued; adalimumab was then discontinued by the patient. In April 2026, left knee swelling recurred, ESR was 37 mm/h and CRP was 1.842 mg/dl, while other joint symptoms were minimal. MRI showed numerous floating particles and T2-low-signal bodies, and arthroscopic exploration confirmed rice-body bursitis of the knee. After arthroscopic debridement, the knee symptoms resolved completely within one week. The two episodes occurred 7 years apart and involved different joints, indicating that rice-body bursitis in RA can present as a metachronous sequential condition. Inflammatory marker levels did not parallel the severity of local joint involvement in this patient. This case underscores that rice-body bursitis should be considered in RA patients with refractory monoarthritis. Arthroscopic clearance combined with systemic antirheumatic therapy was followed by resolution of knee symptoms within one week in this patient. Because the two episodes involved different joints, disease phases, and concurrent treatments, no comparison between treatment strategies can be made.

items.title: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis masquerading as lung cancer with meningeal metastasis: a case report and literature review.
items.abstract: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is an anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated small-vessel vasculitis classically presenting with upper and lower respiratory tract and renal involvement. Central nervous system (CNS) involvement in GPA is rare and is highly prone to being misdiagnosed as intracranial tumor metastasis or intracranial infection. We report a 60-year-old female who presented with recurrent headache and conjunctival injection. She had undergone two surgical procedures for "glaucoma" at an outside hospital without headache relief. Upon admission to our hospital, chest CT revealed multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules, highly suspicious for lung cancer; brain MRI showed dural thickening with subdural effusion; lumbar puncture revealed an intracranial pressure (ICP) of 270 mmH₂O, with negative CSF cultures and no tumor cells. The initial diagnosis was leptomeningeal metastasis from lung cancer. However, percutaneous lung biopsy showed no evidence of tumor or infection, and serology revealed positive c-ANCA/PR3-ANCA, leading to a final diagnosis of GPA with clinicoradiologically supported GPA-related pachymeningitis. After glucocorticoid therapy, the patient's headache and other symptoms resolved rapidly. We reviewed 33 published cases of GPA with cranial involvement and summarized their clinical features. Hypertrophic pachymeningitis (HP) was the most common cranial manifestation (51.5%). Serum ANCA positivity was 87.9% (29/33). Among all 33 cases, c-ANCA/PR3-ANCA was reported in 23 (69.7%); among the 29 ANCA-positive cases, c-ANCA/PR3-ANCA accounted for 79.3% (23/29). After immunosuppressive or immunomodulatory therapy, approximately 90.9% of patients improved or stabilized. These features may serve as clues that should prompt clinicians to consider GPA in the differential diagnosis of pulmonary nodules with pachymeningeal disease and raised intracranial pressure, rather than as established discriminators from lung cancer brain metastasis. GPA can present with multiple pulmonary masses, headache, and pachymeningitis, closely mimicking leptomeningeal metastasis of lung cancer. When imaging and clinical presentation are atypical, serum ANCA testing and pathological biopsy are key to differential diagnosis. Clinicians should be alert to this "mimic of malignancy" to avoid unnecessary surgery or radiotherapy.

items.title: Unravelling IgG4-Related Disease: A Case of Systemic Inflammation and Autoimmune Overlap.
items.abstract: Immunoglobulin G4-related disease (IgG4-RD) is a rare, chronic, immune-mediated disorder characterized by fibroinflammatory changes and infiltration of IgG4-positive plasma cells; its clinical spectrum overlaps with malignancies, infections, and autoimmune conditions, often complicating diagnosis. We report a 47-year-old woman with a history of seronegative rheumatoid arthritis, antiphospholipid syndrome, and diabetes mellitus who presented with low-grade fever, left flank pain, and generalized lymphadenopathy. Laboratory findings revealed markedly elevated CRP and IgG4, and imaging demonstrated pulmonary infiltrates and widespread lymphadenopathy concerning for malignancy. Excisional lymph node biopsy showed plasma cell-rich hyperplasia with increased IgG4-positive plasma cells, and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and cytomegalovirus (CMV) serologies suggested recent or reactivated infection. The patient was diagnosed with IgG4-RD and treated with corticosteroids followed by rituximab, resulting in clinical improvement. This case illustrates the diagnostic complexity of IgG4-RD in the presence of systemic inflammation, autoimmune background, and viral reactivation; its pathogenesis involves atypical immune regulation between B cells and CD4+ cytotoxic T cells that drives cytokine-mediated fibroblast activation, leading to storiform fibrosis and lymphoplasmacytic infiltration. EBV infection may have acted as a trigger for IgG4 class switching, though its role remains uncertain, and early histopathological confirmation with prompt treatment is critical to prevent irreversible organ damage. IgG4-RD should be considered in patients with unexplained systemic lymphadenopathy and elevated inflammatory markers after exclusion of infection and malignancy; a multidisciplinary approach is essential for diagnosis and management, and this case underscores the potential contribution of viral triggers, particularly EBV, warranting further research.

items.title: Vinpocetine ameliorates bone erosion and joint inflammation in rheumatoid arthritis via suppression of NLRP3 inflammasome.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune disease characterized by persistent synovial hyperplasia, cartilage degradation, and bone erosion. Vinpocetine (VIN), a semisynthetic derivative of the alkaloid vincamine, exhibits anti-inflammatory effects. However, the effect of VIN on NLRP3-mediated inflammation in RA remains unclear. In the collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) mouse model, treatment with vinpocetine (VIN) at doses of 5 and 10 mg/kg significantly alleviated characteristic symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis in CIA mice, including joint swelling, reduced grip strength, and mechanical hypersensitivity. Histopathological features of rheumatoid arthritis, such as bone erosion, cartilage destruction, and synovial hyperplasia, were also markedly improved in the CIA + VIN groups. In addition, the mRNA and protein expression levels of RA-associated inflammatory cytokines were significantly elevated in the CIA group but were markedly reduced in both CIA + VIN groups. Notably, VIN significantly suppressed the expression of NLRP3 inflammasome-related factors, including NLRP3, IL-1β, and IL-18, in CIA mice. Furthermore, VIN suppressed NLRP3 expression and inhibited osteoclastogenesis in bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs). This study demonstrates that VIN mitigates structural damage in vivo and reduces joint inflammation by suppressing NLRP3 inflammasome activation in both in vivo and in vitro models, supporting its potential as a therapeutic candidate for rheumatoid arthritis.

items.title: Disease-related readmission in anti-SRP-positive immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy: Incidence and exploratory associated factors in a retrospective cohort study.
items.abstract: Anti-signal recognition particle (anti-SRP)-positive immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) is a severe subtype of idiopathic inflammatory myopathy, but its long-term prognosis and determinants of adverse outcomes remain insufficiently defined. Because relapse is difficult to ascertain consistently in retrospective studies, IMNM-related readmission may serve as a pragmatic outcome for evaluating subsequent disease course. To estimate the incidence rate of IMNM-related readmission after first discharge and to explore factors associated with readmission in patients with anti-SRP-positive IMNM. A single-center retrospective cohort study. We included consecutively hospitalized adults with anti-SRP-positive IMNM at West China Hospital between January 2010 and June 2025. Follow-up began at first discharge. The outcome was readmission attributed to IMNM disease activity. The overall incidence rate was calculated per 100 person-years. Stratified incidence analyses were performed according to baseline variables, and factors associated with readmission were explored using LASSO-penalized Cox regression and univariable Cox regression. Among 131 included patients, 27 experienced IMNM-related readmission during follow-up. The median follow-up was 2.64 years, with a total of 398.53 person-years. The overall incidence rate of IMNM-related readmission was 6.77 per 100 person-years (95% CI, 4.46-9.86). Patients with higher De Ritis ratio (DRR, AST/ALT) had a higher readmission incidence rate than those with lower DRR [9.75 vs 3.28 per 100 person-years; incidence rate ratio (IRR) 2.98, 95% CI 1.24-7.16]. In exploratory univariable Cox regression, DRR was associated with increased readmission risk (HR 3.26, 95% CI 1.49-7.13; P = 0.003). IMNM-related readmission occurred in approximately one-fifth of patients with anti-SRP-positive IMNM during follow-up. Higher DRR was associated with a higher rate of IMNM-related readmission in exploratory analyses. Further prospective studies are needed to clarify the prognostic relevance of DRR and to better characterize the long-term disease course of anti-SRP-positive IMNM. Anti-SRP immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy is a rare autoimmune muscle disease that can cause severe muscle weakness and high muscle enzyme levels. Some patients may worsen again after leaving hospital and need to be readmitted. However, it is difficult to measure disease relapse consistently in retrospective medical records, because symptoms, muscle strength, blood tests, and treatment information are not always recorded in the same way over time. In this study, we reviewed hospitalized adults with anti-SRP immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy treated at West China Hospital. We followed patients from their first hospital discharge and recorded readmissions that were considered to be related to disease activity. We found that disease-related readmission was not uncommon. We also explored whether routinely available clinical features or blood tests were associated with readmission. One blood test measure, the AST/ALT ratio, also called the De Ritis ratio, was higher in patients who were later readmitted. Patients with a higher AST/ALT ratio had a higher rate of disease-related readmission than those with a lower ratio. Because AST and ALT are commonly measured in routine care, this ratio may be a simple marker to help clinicians identify patients who may need closer follow-up after discharge. These findings should be interpreted cautiously. This was a single-center retrospective study, and the number of readmission events was limited. The AST/ALT ratio should therefore be considered a candidate marker rather than a confirmed predictor. Further prospective studies are needed to confirm whether it can help guide follow-up and management in this rare muscle disease.

items.title: Diagnostic value of anti-carbamylated protein combined with Anti-RA33 antibodies in seronegative rheumatoid arthritis: a retrospective cohort study.
items.abstract: Seronegative rheumatoid arthritis (SNRA), defined by the absence of rheumatoid factor (RF) and anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA), poses a persistent diagnostic challenge. Anti-carbamylated protein antibodies (Anti-CarP-IgG) and anti-RA33 antibodies targeting heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein A2/B1 (hnRNP-A2/B1) have been proposed as supplementary biomarkers, yet their combined diagnostic utility in SNRA remains insufficiently characterized. A retrospective cohort study enrolled 550 RA patients (2010 ACR/EULAR criteria) at a single tertiary center (2024-2025). Patients were stratified into SNRA (RF-IgM < 14 IU/mL and ACPA < 5 U/mL; n = 189) and seropositive RA (SPRA; n = 361). Anti-CarP-IgG and Anti-RA33-IgG were measured by ELISA (positivity cutoff > 20 U/mL). Disease activity was assessed by DAS28-ESR/CRP; radiographic damage by modified Sharp/van der Heijde score and Larsen staging. Odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were computed; Bonferroni correction was applied for multiple comparisons. Anti-RA33-IgG positivity was significantly lower in SNRA versus SPRA (15.9% vs. 29.9%, p < 0.001; OR 2.26, 95% CI 1.44-3.55), as was Anti-CarP-IgG positivity (10.6% vs. 23.0%, p = 0.001; OR 2.52, 95% CI 1.49-4.26). Combined testing identified at least one novel antibody in 23.8% of SNRA patients versus 45.2% of SPRA patients (p < 0.001). Within SNRA, Anti-CarP-IgG-positive patients showed significantly more advanced radiographic staging: Stage IV prevalence was 25.0% vs. 7.1% in Anti-CarP-IgG-negative patients (OR 4.36, 95% CI 1.35-14.05, p = 0.021), despite equivalent DAS28-ESR (p = 0.902). Combined Anti-CarP-IgG and Anti-RA33-IgG testing captures serological evidence in nearly one-quarter of SNRA patients. Anti-CarP-IgG positivity associates with a 4.4-fold increased odds of Stage IV radiographic disease, supporting its role as a prognostic stratification tool in SNRA.

items.title: Non-RA screening for systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases using a machine learning model based on physical findings and blood test data.
items.abstract: In patients with systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARDs), particularly patients with non-rheumatoid arthritis (non-RA), the incidence of severe conditions such as interstitial pneumonia and pulmonary arterial hypertension is high. Therefore, early referral of these patients to university hospitals or other institutions capable of comprehensive medical care is desirable. However, the substantial overlap in clinical presentations across SARDs makes differentiation challenging, and objective tools to support disease classification in routine clinical practice remain limited. In this study, a machine learning based classifier was developed to distinguish Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) from non‑RA conditions using general physical findings and routine blood test data, focusing on patients who were diagnosed with a predefined set of SARDs from a secondary‑care teaching hospital. An observational retrospective study was conducted on 571 patients initially diagnosed with SARDs. From the hospital's clinical information database, patients' diagnoses, blood test results, and physical findings were extracted from the hospital's clinical information database to create the dataset. Physical findings were extracted as structured data using natural language processing from medical records written in a free description format by the attending physicians. For patient classification, some non-RA screening model using three classification algorithms were developed: Naive Bayes, Linear Support Vector Machines, and Random Forest. RA and non-RA diseases share common clinical symptoms, with joint symptoms observed in over 40% of patients with the target diseases. Of the screening models, the random forest model performed the best, achieving a sensitivity of 77.3% and a specificity of 72.5%. In this single-center retrospective cohort of patients with confirmed SARDs, a machine learning-based classifier using routinely available clinical symptoms and blood test results demonstrated promising internal performance for differentiating RA from non-RA conditions. These findings support the feasibility of machine learning-based classification within this secondary-care setting. Future studies are needed to validate the model in broader clinical populations, including primary care settings, and to evaluate its potential role in supporting referral decision-making.

items.title: Expression of herpes simplex virus-related genes in peripheral blood leukocytes of patients with behçet's disease: a case-control study.
items.abstract: Behçet's disease is a chronic, relapsing multisystem inflammatory disorder characterized by recurrent oral and genital ulcerations, ocular inflammation, cutaneous lesions, and variable involvement of the vascular, neurological, and gastrointestinal systems. Although its precise etiology remains incompletely understood, accumulating evidence indicates that the disease arises from a complex interplay between genetic susceptibility, immune dysregulation, and environmental triggers. Among the proposed infectious agents, herpes simplex virus (HSV) has attracted considerable attention because of its capacity to induce persistent immune activation, molecular mimicry, and chronic inflammatory responses. Accordingly, the present study aimed to evaluate the expression profiles of HSV-related genes (UL29, UL18, UL46, and UL47) in peripheral blood leukocytes of patients with Behçet's disease to clarify the potential contribution of HSV infection to disease pathogenesis and immune-mediated inflammatory mechanisms. In this case-control study, 40 patients with BD and 40 healthy individuals were included as the control group. Blood samples were collected from all participants. Total RNA was extracted from peripheral blood leukocytes, followed by cDNA synthesis. The expression levels of UL29, UL18, UL46, and UL47 genes were quantified using RT-qPCR. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to assess the diagnostic potential of the studied genes. Statistical analyses were conducted using GraphPad Prism and SPSS software (P-value ≤ 0.05). The expression of HSV-related genes was significantly higher in BD patients compared to healthy controls. After Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, UL29 remained significantly upregulated (4.5-fold, adjusted p = 0.012), while UL46 (3.7-fold, adjusted p = 0.060), UL18 (2.0-fold, adjusted p = 0.152), and UL47 (2.25-fold, p = 0.12) did not reach statistical significance. ROC curve analysis demonstrated strong diagnostic potential for UL29 (AUC = 0.90, sensitivity 80%, specificity 92.5%), UL46 (AUC = 0.86, sensitivity 87%, specificity 77.5%), and UL18 (AUC = 0.80, sensitivity 85%, specificity 72.5%). Overall, UL29, UL46, and UL18 showed promising potential as biomarkers for distinguishing BD patients from healthy individuals. Increased expression of UL29, UL46, and UL18 is associated with BD, and these genes, particularly UL29, show promising potential as diagnostic biomarkers. Further validation studies are needed.

items.title: ISG15 links type I interferon pathway to cardiovascular risk in systemic lupus erythematosus.
items.abstract: Patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) have significantly increased cardiovascular risk, and atherosclerosis (AS) is a major cause of long-term mortality. However, whether SLE-specific immune dysregulation drives accelerated AS remains unclear. This study explored the role of interferon-stimulated gene 15 (ISG15) in SLE-associated AS. We first characterized the disease manifestations, then identified disease characteristics at the proteomic and transcriptomic levels via multi-omics analysis of a pristane-induced SLE-ApoE -/- mouse model and integrated analysis of SLE and AS datasets. We found ISG15 was uniquely elevated across atherosclerotic plaque types and correlated with cardiovascular events, with robust interferon-alpha response activation in SLE mice. Further, ISG15 colocalized with CD68⁺ macrophages in plaques, and extended analysis showed it was highly expressed in peripheral blood monocytes of SLE patients. Clinically, ISG15⁺ monocyte proportion was significantly higher in SLE patients with AS, outperforming conventional cardiovascular risk scores and serving as an independent predictor. In conclusion, ISG15 is a critical effector linking SLE immune dysregulation to accelerated AS, and ISG15⁺ monocyte proportion is a promising biomarker for cardiovascular risk stratification in SLE patients.

items.title: Steroid-responsive Purtscher-like retinopathy associated with macular edema in systemic lupus erythematosus: a case report.
items.abstract: To report a case of Purtscher-like retinopathy (PLR) associated with macular edema in a young person with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) whose vision was restored with a systemic corticosteroid regimen and to highlight the rare and vision-threatening complication of SLE. Case report. A 27-year-old female without significant ophthalmological history who had stopped taking azathioprine and methylprednisolone for her SLE presented with sudden painless unilateral vision loss (best-corrected visual acuity [BCVA] RE: 1 m CF, LE: 20/20). Fundus examination revealed bilateral Purtscher-flecken and cotton wool spots, while optical coherence tomography (OCT) identified intra- and subretinal fluid representing macular edema with paracentral acute middle maculopathy (PAMM) on the right eye. The findings led to PLR diagnosis, and the patient received IV methylprednisolone with tapering. Five months after initial encounter, the patient's vision recovered (BCVA RE: 20/30, LE: 20/20) and OCT showed resolution of the pathology. While PLR is rarely found in people with SLE, it should be considered as a differential diagnosis in people with SLE presenting with sudden vision loss due to the condition being easy to diagnose clinically and its prompt treatment using corticosteroids may restore the vision loss and resolve the retinal pathology.

items.title: A human rheumatoid arthritis bone-cartilage interface organoid recapitulates bone, cartilage, and immune interactions.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by synovial inflammation, cartilage degradation, and bone erosion. Fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLS) play a central role in perpetuating joint damage, yet current therapies inadequately address FLS-driven pathology. Existing preclinical models, including murine collagen-induced arthritis and conventional in vitro cultures, lack the complexity to fully recapitulate human disease mechanisms. Here, we describe the development of a three-dimensional (3D) RA bone-cartilage interface (BCI) organoid that integrates primary human mesenchymal stem cell-derived osteoblasts, peripheral blood mononuclear cell-derived osteoclasts and lymphocytes, immortalized human chondrocyte spheroids, and the RA synovial fibroblast cell line SW982. Exposure to TNF-α, IL-1β, and TGF-β induced pro-inflammatory cytokines, matrix-degrading enzymes, and increased fibrotic gene expression, accompanied by histological and microCT evidence of bone dysregulation. Therapeutic testing showed that methotrexate, etanercept, and tofacitinib reduced cytokine production and pro-inflammatory gene expression but had limited impact on profibrotic gene expression. This modular, human-derived RA BCI organoid reproduced key features of RA pathogenesis that can enable direct assessment of therapeutic mechanisms at the bone-cartilage-synovial interface. The RA BCI organoid provides a physiologically relevant, scalable platform for preclinical drug discovery and for identifying combination strategies that address both the inflammatory and fibrotic components of RA pathology.

items.title: First experience with obinutuzumab in a juvenile-onset systemic lupus erythematosus patient with rituximab-associated posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome.
items.abstract: Juvenile-onset systemic lupus erythematosus (JSLE) is characterized by higher disease activity and greater treatment burden than adult-onset disease, often requiring intensive immunosuppression. Rituximab is used in refractory cases, but re-exposure may not be possible when adverse events such as posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) occur. Obinutuzumab, a type II anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, has shown efficacy in adult patients with lupus nephritis and in those with active SLE, yet pediatric experience is limited. We report an 11-year-old boy with JSLE and lupus nephritis who developed lupus pneumonitis and increased renal activity while receiving conventional therapy. Rituximab was initiated but complicated by PRES six hours after the first infusion, leading to discontinuation. Despite cyclophosphamide induction and mycophenolate mofetil plus cyclosporine maintenance, he later experienced a disease flare with malar rash, low complement levels, and rising anti-dsDNA titres. Because rituximab re-use was avoided, obinutuzumab was selected as an alternative anti-CD20 agent in the setting of a disease flare. A body-surface-area-adjusted regimen derived from the adult protocol was administered in two infusions under close monitoring. Following obinutuzumab, complement levels normalized, anti-dsDNA declined, and SLEDAI-2K decreased from 6 to 2, and peripheral B-cell depletion was confirmed at eight weeks and maintained at six months, without neurological or infectious complications over six months of follow-up. This case suggests that obinutuzumab may be a feasible alternative anti-CD20 option in rituximab-intolerant JSLE, pending results from ongoing pediatric clinical trials.

items.title: Factors Associated With Elevated C-Reactive Protein Levels in Women With Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Followed at the Cocody University Hospital, Abidjan, Côte d'Ivoire.
items.abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune connective tissue disease characterised by multivisceral involvement and the presence of autoantibodies. In this context, C-reactive protein (CRP) holds a particular position: a moderate rise accompanies autoimmune flares, whereas a sharp elevation suggests an infection or specific inflammatory manifestations. This study aimed to analyse the factors associated with increased CRP levels in women with lupus followed at the Cocody University Hospital in Abidjan. This was a cross-sectional observational study including 62 adult women with SLE (ACR/EULAR criteria). Collected variables included socio-demographic, clinical, biological and immunological data. CRP was categorised into three groups: (<6 mg/L, 6-20 mg/L and >20 mg/L). Univariate and multivariate analyses were performed using binary logistic regression, supplemented by the estimation of marginal effects. The results show a mean CRP concentration of 28.2 ± 21.2 mg/L. A CRP level >20 mg/L was common and significantly associated with renal manifestations, arthralgia/arthritis and the severity level of pain. Biologically, proteinuria ≥0.5 g/24 h, hypercreatininemia and leukocytosis were strongly correlated with elevated CRP. In multivariate regression, only hypercreatininemia remained significant (odds ratio [OR] = 24.8; p = 0.011). The estimation of marginal effects confirmed its major impact (+47.5 probability points), as well as that of proteinuria (+31.3 points) and obesity (+14.1 points), while overweight appeared protective (-19.2 points). The SLE Disease Activity Index (SLEDAI) score was positively but modestly correlated with CRP (+1.4 probability points/unit). The model's ROC curve showed excellent performance (area under the ROC curve [AUC] = 0.84). In conclusion, elevated CRP levels were primarily associated with renal manifestations, notably proteinuria and elevated serum creatinine, as well as with disease activity. CRP could therefore serve as a complementary biomarker in the assessment of patients with SLE, particularly in the presence of renal involvement. However, these results should be interpreted as associations and require confirmation by longitudinal studies.

items.title: USP46 restrains K63-linked polyubiquitination-dependent aggregation and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in lupus nephritis.
items.abstract: The activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome necessitates its aggregation within the dispersed trans-Golgi network (dTGN) and subsequent transport from the dTGN to the microtubule organizing center (MTOC), a process facilitated by HDAC6. However, the regulatory mechanisms governing the formation of NLRP3 aggregates remain insufficiently understood. In this study, we demonstrate that proteasome impairment induces polyubiquitination and aggregation of NLRP3 at the MTOC. We demonstrate ubiquitin-specific protease 46 (USP46) as a key factor that recognizes NLRP3 as a substrate and restricts nondegradative K63-linked polyubiquitination at lysine residue K930, thereby preventing excessive aggregation, transport to the MTOC, and inflammasome activation. Furthermore, myeloid-specific knockout of USP46 exacerbates renal injury and inflammation in both lipopolysaccharide-induced-induced endotoxic shock and pristane-induced lupus nephritis models. Our findings provide insights into the regulatory mechanisms underlying the aggresomal activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome.

items.title: Comparative cardiovascular outcomes of IL-6 inhibitors versus rituximab in rheumatoid arthritis: a claims-based observational study.
items.abstract: Interleukin-6 receptor inhibitors (IL-6i), tocilizumab and sarilumab, are FDA-approved therapies for rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Beyond their efficacy in controlling systemic inflammation, growing evidence suggests that IL-6 inhibition may confer cardioprotective effects. This study investigates the long-term cardiovascular outcomes associated with IL-6i in RA patients, comparing IL-6 inhibitors with rituximab and evaluating differences between individual IL-6 inhibitor agents. We conducted an observational cohort study using the TriNetX Linked Network (2010-2025) including adults with RA initiating an IL-6 inhibitor or rituximab and ≥ 2 prescriptions for a drug of interest ≥ 6 months apart. Comparisons were as follows: (1) IL-6 inhibitors (sarilumab, tocilizumab) versus rituximab, and (2) tocilizumab versus sarilumab. Patients receiving both IL-6 inhibitors simultaneously or a non-FDA-approved IL-6 blocker (e.g., siltuximab) were excluded. Outcomes included all-cause mortality, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, heart failure (HF), and venous thromboembolism (VTE) over 5 years. We calculated propensity scores using demographics, cardiovascular risk factors, inflammatory markers, prior TNFi exposure, systemic glucocorticoid use, and conventional DMARDs, and used scores to match exposed individuals 1:1 with comparators. Cox models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) for mortality and cardiovascular outcomes individually. All analyses were conducted using the TriNetX platform. After matching, 4288 RA patients per group were included for IL-6i versus rituximab and 605 per group for sarilumab versus tocilizumab. Compared to rituximab, IL-6i was associated with lower hazards of mortality (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.55-0.82), MACE (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.64-0.85), and HF risk (HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.69-0.94), with no significant difference in MI, stroke, or VTE. Amongst IL-6 inhibitors, sarilumab was associated with lower hazards of all-cause mortality compared to tocilizumab (HR 0.52, 95% CI 0.29-0.94), but no significant differences were identified for other cardiovascular outcomes. Among adults with RA, IL-6i use was associated with lower rates of all-cause mortality, MACE, and heart failure compared to rituximab, while risks of stroke, MI, and VTE were similar. A lower risk of all-cause mortality was observed with sarilumab compared to tocilizumab. These findings support a potential survival and cardiovascular benefit of IL-6i and highlight the need for larger studies to further distinguish the cardiovascular outcomes with IL-6i agents. Such evidence could inform personalized treatment decisions based on cardiovascular risk factors. Key Points • This study provides long-term real-world evidence that IL-6 inhibitors may offer superior cardiovascular outcomes compared with rituximab in RA patients previously managed with TNFi, an important evidence gap in biologic choice after TNFi failure. • This study directly compares cardiovascular outcomes between sarilumab and tocilizumab, identifying a potential lower myocardial infarction risk with sarilumab.

items.title: Clinical phenotype, disease burden and inter-regional heterogeneity of axial spondyloarthritis in 1112 patients across 15 Arab countries: the PROSPA study.
items.abstract: To characterise the phenotype, disease burden, comorbidities, patient-reported outcomes (PROs) and treatment patterns of axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) across Arab countries and evaluate regional heterogeneity. Profile of Axial Spondyloarthritis in Arab Countries (PROSPA), a cross-sectional, multinational study by the ArLAR Research Group across 33 rheumatology centres in 15 countries, enrolled adults with axSpA during a routine visit. Standardised data on validated PROs, disease characteristics, comorbidities and treatment were collected. Patients were stratified by Arab subregion (North Africa, the Levant and the Gulf). Between-group comparisons used Welch analysis of variance, Kruskal-Wallis and χ 2 tests. Mixed-effects modelling tested whether regional differences in Assessment of SpondyloArthritis international Society Health Index (ASAS-HI) remained independent after adjustment. Of 1112 patients (mean age 42.6 years, median disease duration 10 years, 63.8% male), radiographic (r) predominated over non-radiographic (nr) axSpA (r/nr ratio 3.7). Peripheral arthritis occurred in 45.7%, coxitis in 31.7%, uveitis in 16.7% and psoriasis in 17.4%. Human leucocyte antigen B27 was positive in 51.5% of 615 tested. Disease activity was moderate to high; biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (bDMARDs) were used in 70.1%, 36.4% were people who smoke and 5.2% had a tuberculosis history. North Africa had the highest r/nr ratio, worst PROs and lowest bDMARD use, despite comparable disease activity. Regional differences in ASAS-HI did not persist after adjustment; disease activity and function accounted for most explained variance. This largest multinational axSpA study revealed a predominantly radiographic phenotype, significant disease burden and a comorbidity profile marked by high smoking and tuberculosis rates. After adjustment, region was not independently associated with ASAS-HI; disease activity and function, rather than geography, explained most of the variance in health status.

items.title: Triggers of Gout Flares from Local to Systemic Perspectives.
items.abstract: Gout is the most common type of inflammatory arthritis, caused by MSU crystal deposition in the joint, resulting from chronic hyperuricemia. Typically, the first clinical presentation is a gout flare characterized by severe pain, redness, joint swelling, and limited mobility. Despite continuous exposure to increased serum urate concentration followed by MSU crystal formation, flares are unpredictable and intermittent when poorly managed. Acute gout flares follow a two-step model: firstly, MSU crystals build up and, secondly, an endogenous or exogenous triggering event is needed. Once both triggers are given, resident macrophages initiate an acute inflammatory response. However, these additional factors are still under debate and increased serum urate concentrations alone are insufficient to ignite gout flares. In this review, we aim to sharpen our understanding of the unique characteristics responsible for transitioning from an asymptomatic state to acute joint inflammation observed in gout patients. We focus on integrating joint mechanisms during a gout flare, such as NLRP3 inflammasome activation, macrophage heterogeneity changes, and local physicochemical conditions with systemic influences from immunometabolism and genetic variation to explain the interindividual variability in flare susceptibility.

items.title: Zooming in on anti-Zo-positive antisynthetase syndrome: A multicenter case series and literature review.
items.abstract: To describe a case series of anti-Zo-positive antisynthetase syndrome (ASyS), as detected by immunoprecipitation-mass spectrometry (IP-MS), and compare the clinical features to previously described cases. Patients with compatible HEp-2 IIF findings or clinical features were screened with IP-MS for anti-Zo autoantibodies. Clinical data were extracted from the patients' electronic health record. A literature review was performed and clinical features of all cases described thus far were summarized. Seven patients with anti-Zo autoantibodies were identified through IP-MS. Both alpha and beta subunits were precipitated and identified. ASyS features were present in all. ILD was the most common manifestation (6/7). In four patients sclerodactyly or other systemic sclerosis-like features were present. A literature review identified 12 more cases as detected by immunoprecipitation-based methods. In this total of 19 patients, ILD and myositis were the most prevalent manifestations, but SSc-like features were also present in 5/19. IP-MS is a reliable detection method for anti-Zo autoantibodies. Anti-Zo-positive ASyS is characterized by typical ASyS features, but in some patients SSc-like features can be present.

items.title: Management of Rheumatoid Arthritis with Individualized Homeopathy: A Prospective, Non-Randomized, Single-Group Interventional Study.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic inflammatory disorder requiring long-term management. Individualized homeopathy has been proposed as a potential adjunct in integrative care, though clinical evidence is limited. The primary objective of the study was to evaluate the effect of homeopathic medicines in the management of RA using the Disease Activity Score 28 (DAS28). The secondary objective aimed to evaluate the activity profile and quality of life of patients using the American College of Rheumatology 20 (ACR20) response criteria. A multi-center, prospective, non-randomized, single-group interventional RA study included 134 patients diagnosed according to the 2010 ACR/European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) criteria. Prescriptions were individualized based on classical homeopathic principles. The primary outcome, DAS28, was assessed at baseline and every 3 months for 12 months. Secondary outcomes were ACR20 response criteria measured monthly, covering tender and swollen joint counts, patient and physician global assessments, pain, and disability. The study was registered with the Clinical Trials Registry-India (CTRI/2018/01/011192). Of the 134 enrolled participants, 74 (55.2%) completed the 12-month follow-up for per-protocol analysis, reflecting 44.8% attrition. Statistically significant improvements ( p  < 0.01) were observed in DAS28 and ACR20 parameters. The baseline DAS28 score (5.03) indicated that the study sample had moderate-to-high RA disease activity, decreasing by 1.26 points at 9 months and by 1.31 points at 12 months, reflecting an improvement over time. ACR20 response included a 40% reduction in tender joints, 90% reduction in swollen joints, and improvements in patient global assessment (77%), physician global assessment (77%), pain (75%), and disability (65%). Symptomatic assessments supported these outcomes. Rhus toxicodendron , Pulsatilla , and Phosphorus were commonly prescribed medicines. Individualized homeopathic treatment resulted in positive outcomes for disease activity and patient-reported outcomes over 12 months, without disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug use. Findings suggest a potential role for individualized homeopathy in integrative RA management, warranting further investigation in controlled trials.

items.title: Citrullination of fibrinogen induced by Porphyromonas gingivalis serve as a key pathway in breaking immune tolerance in rheumatoid arthritis.
items.abstract: This study investigates how Porphyromonas gingivalis (P. gingivalis) breaks immune tolerance to citrullinated antigens in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and characterizes the immunogenicity of citrullinated fibrinogen generated by its secreted peptidylarginine deiminase (PPAD). Subgingival microbiota from ACPA-positive/negative RA patients and healthy controls were profiled by 16S rRNA sequencing and qPCR. Collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) mice were orally colonized with wild-type P. gingivalis W83 or a PPAD-knockout strain, with arthritis severity, histopathology, and immune responses assessed. An in vitro citrullination system was used to produce modified fibrinogen, whose binding to ACPA, macrophage activation, and in vivo immunogenicity were evaluated. P. gingivalis was enriched in ACPA-positive RA patients, correlating with anti-CCP titers and disease activity. Wild-type, but not PPAD-knockout, P. gingivalis exacerbated CIA, boosting anti-CCP levels and splenic B cells. Fibrinogen was the primary substrate upregulated for citrullination in gingiva. The resulting citrullinated fibrinogen formed immune complexes with ACPA that drove M1 macrophage polarization via the TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB pathway. In vivo, this modified protein induced anti-CCP antibodies and aggravated arthritis; proteolytically cleaved fragments demonstrated even greater immunogenicity. By secreting PPAD to citrullinate oral fibrinogen, P. gingivalis initiates systemic autoimmunity and promotes ACPA-positive RA. This work strengthens the mucosal origin hypothesis and provides new targets for early intervention.

items.title: Integrative analysis reveals shared biomarkers and pathways in osteoporosis and rheumatoid arthritis using machine learning and single-cell sequencing.
items.abstract: Osteoporosis (OP) and Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) are prevalent chronic diseases characterized by bone loss and immune dysregulation. Evidence suggests that patients with RA are at increased risk of developing OP; however, the shared molecular mechanisms linking these conditions remain incompletely understood. Publicly available bulk transcriptomic and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets for OP and RA were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) was applied to identify shared gene modules associated with both diseases. Functional enrichment and protein-protein interaction analyses were performed to characterize common biological pathways. Machine learning algorithms, including Random Forest (RF) and Support Vector Machine (SVM), were used to identify and validate shared hub genes and to construct diagnostic models. Immune cell infiltration was evaluated using CIBERSORT, and the cellular localization of hub genes was further validated using scRNA-seq analysis. WGCNA identified 329 genes shared between OP- and RA-associated modules, which were significantly enriched in muscle-related processes, cytokine signaling, and immune-inflammatory pathways. RF analysis identified three shared candidate genes: ANO5, IL27RA, and CNTN3. Among these, ANO5 and IL27RA demonstrated consistent expression evidence and literature support, whereas CNTN3 emerged as a computationally nominated candidate requiring cautious interpretation and experimental validation. An SVM-based model incorporating these genes demonstrated robust predictive accuracy in both OP and RA validation cohorts. Immune infiltration analysis revealed distinct yet coordinated immune landscapes, with hub genes showing significant correlations with T cells, macrophages, B cells, and plasma cells. ScRNA-seq analysis revealed that ANO5 was predominantly expressed in macrophages and fibroblasts, IL27RA was mainly enriched in T cells, whereas CNTN3 showed minimal enrichment at the single-cell level in both OP bone and RA synovial tissues. This integrative bioinformatics and machine learning study identifies shared molecular signatures and immune-related mechanisms underlying OP and RA. ANO5 and IL27RA emerge as robust candidate regulators linking immune dysregulation and bone remodeling, whereas CNTN3-although identified by machine learning-requires cautious interpretation and further investigation due to limited supporting evidence. These findings provide novel insights into the pathogenesis of RA-associated OP and highlight potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets for their comorbidity.

items.title: Nationwide trends in physical disability among rheumatoid arthritis patients in Korea (2010-2022): A retrospective cohort study based on national registry data.
items.abstract: Whether the burden of legally certified disability among patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) has decreased in the modern treatment era is uncertain, particularly in Asia. We investigated trends in registered and physical disability among Korean patients with RA. Using National Health Insurance Service data (patient-level 50% random sample), we identified patients aged ≥19 years with seropositive RA registered in the copayment assistance program for rare and intractable diseases in 2010-2022. Disability status, including physical disability (certified musculoskeletal impairment), came from the national disability registry. We estimated annual prevalence and, in newly diagnosed patients, incidence per 1,000 person-years, and compared the results with national disability statistics. The number of patients with seropositive RA identified in the database and included in this study was 33,992 in 2010 and 67,844 in 2022. The prevalence of registered disability declined from 20.3% to 14.6% and that of physical disability from 17.4% to 10.9% (both p for trend <0.001) in both sexes. Among 61,086 newly diagnosed patients, the incidence of registered disability did not change (5.08 per 1,000 person-years; annual change -0.9%, p = 0.24), whereas that of physical disability declined by 6.7% per year (p < 0.001). Men had a higher incidence of registered disability than women (6.73 vs. 4.58 per 1,000 person-years), but not of physical disability. Older age (odds ratio [OR] 1.035 per year, 95% CI 1.032-1.039), male sex (OR 1.295, 95% CI 1.174-1.429), and lower income were associated with incident registered disability. In 2022, physical disability remained more prevalent in RA (10.9%) than in the general population (2.3%) and in those aged ≥65 years (7.1%). Certified physical disability among Korean patients with RA declined substantially between 2010 and 2022, whereas the incidence of any registered disability remained stable. An excess burden of physical disability compared with the general population persisted.

items.title: Olfactory function in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and its association with disease activity: a cross-sectional case-control study.
items.abstract: The aim of this study was to evaluate odor identification and odor threshold in patients with rheumatoid arthritis, compare these measures with those of healthy controls, and investigate their associations with disease activity. This cross-sectional case-control study with prospective participant recruitment included patients with rheumatoid arthritis and age- and sex-matched healthy controls. Odor identification (OI) was assessed using the 12-item Rapid Sniffin' Sticks test, and odor threshold (OT) was assessed using the modified CCCRC n-butanol test. Disease duration, disease activity scores, and inflammatory markers, including C-reactive protein (CRP), were recorded. Associations between olfactory measures and disease-related parameters were analyzed. The distribution of odor threshold categories differed significantly between groups (p < 0.001), with higher proportions of anosmia and hyposmia in patients with rheumatoid arthritis than in healthy controls. Odor identification scores did not differ significantly between groups. No statistically significant associations were observed between OT categories or OI scores and disease duration, disease activity scores, or CRP levels. OI scores were higher among methotrexate users than non-users, whereas OT category distribution did not differ significantly according to methotrexate use. Neither olfactory measure was significantly associated with corticosteroid use. Rheumatoid arthritis was associated with an altered distribution of odor threshold categories, whereas odor identification scores did not differ significantly between groups. No statistically significant associations were observed between the olfactory measures and disease activity, disease duration, or CRP levels. These findings do not establish causality or independence from potential confounders. III. Key Points • Patients with rheumatoid arthritis had higher proportions of anosmia and hyposmia than healthy controls. • Odor identification scores did not differ significantly between patients with rheumatoid arthritis and healthy controls. • No statistically significant associations were observed between odor threshold categories or odor identification scores and disease activity, disease duration, or CRP levels. • Rheumatoid arthritis was associated with an altered distribution of odor threshold categories; the independence and causal nature of this association remain to be established.

items.title: Impact of radiographic damage on health-related outcomes across rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and hand osteoarthritis: a comparative analysis of disease burden.
items.abstract: To evaluate the comparative impact of radiographic joint damage on hand functions, objective grip strength, and quality of life across patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), psoriatic arthritis (PsA), and hand osteoarthritis (OA). This cross-sectional study included patients with RA (n = 50), PsA (n = 40), and hand OA (n = 40). Objective grip strength was measured using a calibrated JAMAR hydraulic dynamometer. Radiographic damage was assessed using the modified Total Sharp Score (mTSS) for inflammatory cohorts and the Kellgren-Lawrence (K-L) scale for hand OA. Functional status and psychosocial impact were evaluated through Duruöz Hand Index (DHI), Quick Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder, and Hand (QuickDASH) questionnaire, Health Assessment Questionnaire (HAQ), and the Short Form-36 (SF-36) Health Survey scales. Spearman correlation analyses and adjusted multivariable linear regression models were performed to evaluate the relationship between radiographic damage and functional outcomes. Despite marked differences in disease duration, radiographic damage, and treatment profiles, objectively measured grip strength and patient-reported hand disability did not differ significantly among the three disease groups (all p > 0.05). In unadjusted analyses, greater radiographic damage was associated with lower grip strength in PsA (r = - 0.405, 95% CI - 0.637 to - 0.107), but not with QuickDASH or DHI; no significant associations between radiographic damage and these functional outcomes were observed in RA or hand OA. After multivariable adjustment, high radiographic damage remained associated with lower grip strength in PsA (β = - 9.02, 95% CI - 17.19 to - 0.85), but was not associated with QuickDASH or DHI. Disease activity was most strongly associated with functional outcomes in RA, whereas radiographic severity was not independently associated with grip strength or patient-reported hand function in hand OA. Grip strength was inversely correlated with hand-specific patient-reported outcomes across all disease groups. Although patients with RA, PsA, and hand OA experience comparable levels of hand dysfunction, the factors associated with functional impairment differ according to disease phenotype. Structural damage appears to have a greater influence on objective hand performance in PsA, whereas disease activity predominates in RA and radiographic severity alone does not explain disability in hand OA. These findings highlight the importance of disease-specific interpretation of structural damage and support comprehensive functional assessment in patients with inflammatory and degenerative hand arthritis. Key Points • Patients with RA, psoriatic arthritis, and hand OA exhibited comparable levels of objectively measured grip strength and patient-reported hand disability despite substantial differences in disease duration and radiographic severity. • Multivariable analyses demonstrated disease-specific determinants of functional impairment: radiographic damage was independently associated with reduced grip strength only in psoriatic arthritis, whereas disease activity was the principal factor associated with functional outcomes in RA and radiographic severity alone did not explain disability in hand OA. • Functional impairment in hand OA cannot be explained solely by structural radiographic changes, underscoring the need for comprehensive functional assessment beyond conventional imaging findings.

items.title: Coexistence of systemic lupus erythematosus and IgG4-related disease: a case report and literature review.
items.abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic multisystem autoimmune disease with diverse clinical and serological manifestations. IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD) is a systemic fibroinflammatory condition characterized by mass-forming lesions, dense IgG4-positive plasma cell infiltration, storiform fibrosis, and obliterative phlebitis. Although rare, cases of SLE coexisting with IgG4-RD have been reported. We report a 44-year-old woman with a 15-year history of SLE with serositis, articular, and mucocutaneous involvement, who developed a painless mass in the left submandibular gland. Histopathological evaluation revealed dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, storiform fibrosis, and obliterative phlebitis, with 97 IgG4 + plasma cells per high-power field and an IgG4/IgG ratio of 63%. Serum IgG4 was mildly elevated and was considered supportive rather than diagnostic. These findings supported a diagnosis of IgG4-RD. A literature review identified nine cases of SLE/IgG4-RD overlap; in most cases, the diagnoses of SLE and IgG4-RD were established concomitantly, whereas only a single report described IgG4-RD developing subsequent to SLE. In conclusion, the coexistence of SLE and IgG4-RD is possible. Recognition of this overlap is essential for individualized treatment strategies targeting both conditions. Key Points • IgG4-related disease can develop in patients with long-standing, established systemic lupus erythematosus.. • Non-fulfillment of the 2019 ACR/EULAR IgG4-RD classifi cation criteria, driven by SLE-associated serological exclusions, should not be used to exclude clinicopathologically confirmed coexistence. • Elevated serum IgG4 or IgG4+ plasma cells alone are insufficient to diagnose IgG4-RD in SLE; histopathology, quantitative immunostaining, and exclusion of mimickers are required. • None of the nine published SLE/IgG4-RD overlap cases fulfilled the IgG4-RD classification criteria.
